_comment: Exercises taken from the twelve lecture notebooks (fin400/lectures/). Each lecture keeps its own notebook; these are the tasks inside them, with hints and hidden checks but no worked answer.

problems.title: Lecture 01 · Exercise 1 — Load the monthly file and count what is in it
problems.prompt:
`fin400-monthly-stocks.csv` is one row per stock per month: `permno`, `caldt`,
`ticker`, `prc`, `ret` and `mcap`.

Load it into `data` with `caldt` parsed as a date. Then keep
`months = data['caldt'].nunique()` and `stocks = data['permno'].nunique()`, and print
both on their own line.

Before you plot anything or average anything, this is the check that the file
arrived intact.
hints: `parse_dates=["caldt"]` belongs inside `pd.read_csv(...)`.
`.nunique()` counts distinct values in a column.
Two `print` calls, so two lines: the month count first, then the stock count.
problems.tests:
assert data.shape == (5400, 6)
assert months == 120
assert stocks == 45
assert str(data["caldt"].dtype).startswith("datetime64")
problems.test_summary: the file loads, the date is a date, and the counts are right

problems.title: Lecture 01 · Exercise 2 — How many rows, and which years
problems.prompt:
Type exactly what this program prints, one line per `print`. Work it out from the
file's description rather than running it: 45 stocks observed every month for ten
years, starting in January 1926.
hints: `len(data)` is the number of rows, not the number of columns.
`.min()` on a date column gives the earliest date; `.dt.year` takes the year from it.
Three lines: a row count and two years.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("fin400-monthly-stocks.csv", parse_dates=["caldt"])

print(len(data))
print(data["caldt"].min().year)
print(data["caldt"].max().year)

problems.title: Lecture 02 · Exercise 1 — Natural logs of a list, in a function
problems.prompt:
Write `loglist(values)` that returns a new list holding the natural log of every
value, in the same order. Then print `loglist([2.718281828459045, 1, 10])`.

The list you return must have the same length as the list you were given.
hints: Import `math` and call `math.log(x)` inside the loop.
Build an empty list first, append inside the loop, and return the list at the end.
`math.log(math.e)` is 1.0, which makes a quick mental check.
problems.tests:
out = loglist([2.718281828459045, 1, 10])
assert len(out) == 3
assert abs(out[0] - 1.0) < 1e-9
assert abs(out[1] - 0.0) < 1e-12
assert abs(out[2] - 2.302585092994046) < 1e-9
assert loglist([]) == []
problems.test_summary: one natural log per value, same order, same length

problems.title: Lecture 02 · Exercise 2 — The log of a list is not a number
problems.prompt:
This program should print the natural log of each value:
`[1.0, 0.0, 2.302585092994046]`. Instead it raises
`TypeError: must be real number, not list`.

The loop is right and the list handling is right. One name inside `append(...)`
is wrong.
hints: `math.log` takes one number, not the whole list.
The loop variable `x` already holds the value you want to transform.
Change `math.log(pos)` to `math.log(x)`.
problems.starter_code:
import math

pos = [2.718281828459045, 1, 10]
new = []
for x in pos:
    new.append(math.log(pos))

print(new)
problems.tests:
assert len(new) == 3
assert abs(new[0] - 1.0) < 1e-9
assert abs(new[1] - 0.0) < 1e-12
assert abs(new[2] - 2.302585092994046) < 1e-9
problems.test_summary: each value is logged once, so the list has three numbers

problems.title: Lecture 03 · Exercise 1 — The maximum that answers zero for negative returns
problems.prompt:
`find_max(values)` should return the largest value in the list. It works on
`[1, 3, 20, 10, 0.5, 2]` — it returns 20 — but on `[-1, -3, -20, -10, -0.5, -2]` it
returns `0`, a number that is not in the list at all.

Fix the line that starts the running maximum. The loop and the comparison are fine.
hints: The running maximum starts at `0`, so nothing negative can ever beat it.
Start from a value that is actually in the list: the first one.
`maximum = values[0]` — one line, nothing else changes.
problems.test_summary: the running maximum is primed with a value from the list

problems.title: Lecture 03 · Exercise 2 — Mean, median and quartiles by hand
problems.prompt:
Type exactly what this program prints, one line per `print`. The list is
`[21, 23, 24, 25, 26]` — add the five numbers before you reach for a calculator.
hints: The total is 119, and there are five values.
Sorted, the middle value is 24.
Inclusive quartiles split the sorted list at 25% and 75% counting both ends.
problems.starter_code:
import statistics as s

commute = [21, 23, 24, 25, 26]

print(s.mean(commute))
print(s.median(commute))
print(s.quantiles(commute, n=4, method="inclusive"))

problems.title: Lecture 04 · Exercise 1 — Squared deviations, then check them against the variance
problems.prompt:
Write `sqdevs(values)` that returns the squared deviation of every value from the mean
of the list, in the same order.

Check yourself: the mean of the list you return equals
`statistics.pvariance(values)`, because variance is the average squared deviation.
hints: `xbar = statistics.mean(values)` once, outside the loop.
`(x - xbar) ** 2` — parentheses matter; the difference is squared, not the value.
The returned list is the same length as the input.
problems.tests:
assert sqdevs([2, 4, 6]) == [4.0, 0.0, 4.0]
assert abs(sum(sqdevs([1, 2, 3, 4])) / 4 - 1.25) < 1e-12
out = sqdevs([10, 12, 14])
assert len(out) == 3 and abs(sum(out) / 3 - 8 / 3) < 1e-12
assert all(v >= 0 for v in out)
problems.test_summary: each value becomes the square of its distance from the mean

problems.title: Lecture 04 · Exercise 2 — Fill in the percentile lookup
problems.prompt:
Fill in the two blanks so the program prints the value with 5% of a normal
distribution below it, for a mean of 23 and a standard deviation of 3.9.

The first blank is the class, the second is the method that takes a probability.
hints: `statistics.NormalDist(mu, sigma)` builds the distribution.
`cdf` goes from value to probability; you need the other direction.
It is `inv_cdf` — inverse cumulative distribution function.
problems.starter_code:
import statistics as s

nd = s.___(mu=23, sigma=3.9)
print(round(nd.___(0.05), 2))

problems.title: Lecture 05 · Exercise 1 — A CDF for every value in the list
problems.prompt:
Write `listcdf(data, mu, sigma)` that returns a list holding the probability of
being at or below each value in `data`, given a normal distribution with mean
`mu` and standard deviation `sigma`.

Then print `listcdf([23], 23, 3.9)` — the mean has half the distribution below it.

The distribution is built **once** for the whole list, not once per value.
hints: `nd = statistics.NormalDist(mu=mu, sigma=sigma)` before the loop.
Append `nd.cdf(x)` for each `x` in `data`.
Return the list; do not print inside the function.
problems.tests:
out = listcdf([23], 23, 3.9)
assert len(out) == 1 and abs(out[0] - 0.5) < 1e-12
assert abs(listcdf([19], 23, 3.9)[0] - 0.152525) < 1e-5
assert len(listcdf([1, 2, 3], 2, 1)) == 3
assert listcdf([], 0, 1) == []
problems.test_summary: one probability per value, from a single distribution

problems.title: Lecture 05 · Exercise 2 — Three lines from a loop over positions
problems.prompt:
Type exactly what this program prints — three lines, one per value, in the order the
loop walks the list.

The probabilities are the same ones from the lecture: a value equal to the mean has
0.5 below it.
hints: `range(len(data))` gives 0, 1, 2.
Each line prints the position, the value and the probability, separated by spaces.
problems.starter_code:
import statistics as s

data = [19.0, 23.0, 27.0]
nd = s.NormalDist(mu=23, sigma=3.9)
cdfs = [nd.cdf(x) for x in data]

for i in range(len(data)):
    print(i, data[i], round(cdfs[i], 4))

problems.title: Lecture 06 · Exercise 1 — Bucket the equal-weight return series
problems.prompt:
Load `fin400-monthly-stocks.csv`, build the equal-weight portfolio return for each
month (`ew`), and put those returns — in **percent** — into four buckets:
`[-100, -5, 0, 5, 100]`.

Print the share of months in each bucket, as a percentage rounded to one decimal,
in bucket order.
hints: `ew = data.groupby("caldt")["ret"].mean()` gives one return per month.
`pd.cut(ew * 100, [...])` labels each month with its bucket.
`bins.value_counts().sort_index() / len(ew) * 100` is the share in percent.
problems.tests:
assert len(ew) == 120
assert abs(float(ew.mean()) * 100 - 0.86) < 0.01
assert len(bins.cat.categories) == 4
assert int(bins.value_counts().sum()) == 120
assert abs(float(share.sum()) - 100) < 0.2
problems.test_summary: one portfolio return per month, every month in exactly one bucket

problems.title: Lecture 06 · Exercise 2 — Four bucket counts
problems.prompt:
Type exactly what this program prints: the count of months in each bucket, in bucket
order. The four numbers add up to the 120 months in the file.
hints: `sort_index()` prints the buckets from the lowest to the highest.
`value_counts()` counts the months that fell into each bucket.
One print per bucket because the loop walks `share.items()`.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("fin400-monthly-stocks.csv", parse_dates=["caldt"])
ew = data.groupby("caldt")["ret"].mean()
bins = pd.cut(ew * 100, [-100, -5, 0, 5, 100])
counts = bins.value_counts().sort_index()

for bucket, count in counts.items():
    print(count)

problems.title: Lecture 07 · Exercise 1 — Two new columns from two old ones
problems.prompt:
Load `fin400-stock-panel.csv` into `df`. Add `eps` = `ni / shr` (net income per share)
and `mult` = `mcap / ni` (market value per dollar of net income).

Then print `df[['ni', 'eps', 'mult']].describe()`.

Both columns come from arithmetic on columns that are already there.
hints: Assign a new column with `df['eps'] = ...`.
Column arithmetic is elementwise, so no loop is needed.
`describe()` on a list of columns gives one row per statistic, one column per variable.
problems.tests:
assert len(df) == 2343
assert abs(float(df["eps"].median()) - 4.222102) < 1e-3
assert abs(float(df["mult"].median()) - float((df["mcap"] / df["ni"]).median())) < 1e-9
assert df["eps"].notna().all()
problems.test_summary: eps and mult are built from the columns already in the file

problems.title: Lecture 07 · Exercise 2 — Fill in the percentile call
problems.prompt:
Fill in the two blanks so the program prints the 10th and 90th percentile of `eps`
for the stock panel.
hints: The `Series` method is `quantile`.
Probabilities are decimals: the 10th percentile is `0.1`.
It takes a list to return several percentiles at once.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("fin400-stock-panel.csv")
df["eps"] = df["ni"] / df["shr"]

print(df["eps"].___([___, 0.9]).round(2).tolist())

problems.title: Lecture 08 · Exercise 1 — Men aged 40 and over
problems.prompt:
Load `fin400-survey.csv` into `df` and add a `bmi` column: weight in kilograms over
height in metres squared.

Then keep `older_men` — the rows where `gender` is `'male'` **and** `age` is at least
40 — and print `older_men['bmi'].mean()`.

The file spells the categories out in words.
hints: `df['bmi'] = df['weight'] / (df['height'] / 100) ** 2`.
Two conditions need `&`, with each comparison in parentheses.
`gender` is `'male'` or `'female'` — check `df['gender'].unique()` if unsure.
problems.tests:
assert len(df) == 900
assert int((df["gender"] == "male").sum()) == 420
assert len(older_men) < len(df)
assert (older_men["gender"] == "male").all()
assert (older_men["age"] >= 40).all()
assert abs(float(older_men["bmi"].mean()) - float(df.loc[(df["gender"] == "male") & (df["age"] >= 40), "bmi"].mean())) < 1e-9
problems.test_summary: the subset is male and at least 40, and the mean is of that subset

problems.title: Lecture 08 · Exercise 2 — Two conditions joined with `and`
problems.prompt:
The program raises `ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous` before it
prints anything.

The conditions are the right ones. The operator between them is not.
hints: `and` is for single True/False values; a Series has one per row.
pandas uses the elementwise operators `&` and `|`.
Keep each comparison in parentheses: `(a) & (b)`.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("fin400-survey.csv")
df["bmi"] = df["weight"] / (df["height"] / 100) ** 2

subset = df[(df["gender"] == "male") and (df["age"] >= 40)]
print(round(subset["bmi"].mean(), 4))
problems.tests:
assert (subset["gender"] == "male").all()
assert (subset["age"] >= 40).all()
assert 0 < len(subset) < len(df)
assert abs(float(subset["bmi"].mean()) - float(df.loc[(df["gender"] == "male") & (df["age"] >= 40), "bmi"].mean())) < 1e-9
problems.test_summary: both conditions are applied to every row at once

problems.title: Lecture 11 · Exercise 1 — Union of two conditions
problems.prompt:
Load `fin400-monthly-stocks.csv` with `caldt` parsed into `data`.

Keep `either` — the rows from 1926 **or** from the ticker `XKKE` — and print
`len(either)` followed by `either['ticker'].nunique()`.

Either condition is enough to keep a row.
hints: Use `|` between the two conditions, each in parentheses.
`data['caldt'].dt.year == 1926` needs the date parsed first.
`.nunique()` counts distinct values in the filtered frame.
problems.tests:
assert len(data) == 5400
assert int((data["caldt"].dt.year == 1926).sum()) == 540
assert len(either) == 648
assert either["ticker"].nunique() == 45
assert ((either["caldt"].dt.year == 1926) | (either["ticker"] == "XKKE")).all()
problems.test_summary: a row is kept when either condition holds, and counted once

problems.title: Lecture 11 · Exercise 2 — Counting rows by date
problems.prompt:
Type exactly what this program prints. The file covers 45 stocks, every month, from
January 1926 to December 1935.
hints: Rows in 1926: 45 stocks × 12 months.
`nunique()` on the months of 1926 counts months, not rows.
Two lines.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("fin400-monthly-stocks.csv", parse_dates=["caldt"])
in_1926 = data[data["caldt"].dt.year == 1926]

print(len(in_1926))
print(in_1926["caldt"].dt.month.nunique())

problems.title: Lecture 12 · Exercise 1 — Median age and BMI by gender
problems.prompt:
Load `fin400-survey.csv`, add a `bmi` column, and keep
`by_gender = df.groupby('gender')[['age', 'bmi']].median()`. Print it.

One call should give both variables for both groups.
hints: `groupby('gender')` splits the frame; the list in brackets picks the columns.
`.median()` is the aggregation — the mean would be pulled by outliers.
The result is a small table: two rows, two columns.
problems.tests:
assert list(by_gender.index) == ["female", "male"]
assert abs(float(by_gender.loc["male", "bmi"]) - 29.1618) < 1e-3
assert abs(float(by_gender.loc["female", "age"]) - 43.0) < 1e-9
assert list(by_gender.columns) == ["age", "bmi"]
problems.test_summary: one median per gender for both age and bmi

problems.prompt:

hints: The aggregation is the median, not the mean.
Two grouping keys go in a list: `groupby([...])`.
The income column is called `hincome`.
problems.starter_code:
